name: rtk
description: CLI proxy that reduces LLM token consumption by 60-90% on common dev commands. Single Rust binary, zero dependencies
readmeExcerpt:
Agent-agnostic token optimization: compress, route, filter, and more.

One composable pipeline across everything your AI agent reads and sends — built on RTK's battle-tested bash-output compression (up to 90% smaller).

Website • Install • Troubleshooting • Architecture • Discord

English • Francais • 中文 • 日本語 • 한국어 • Espanol • Português

---

rtk filters and compresses command outputs before they reach your LLM context. Single Rust binary, 100+ supported commands, <10ms overhead. ## What RTK Does RTK intercepts shell commands and compresses their output before your agent reads it. | Operation | What RTK does to the output | |-----------|-----------------------------| | `ls` / `tree` | Tree format with file counts instead of one line per entry | | `cat` / `read` | Smart file reading: signatures and structure over full bodies | | `grep` / `rg` | Truncates long lines, groups matches by file | | `ast-grep` | Groups structural matches by file, caps overflow | | `git status` | Compact stat format, grouped by state | | `git diff` | Reduced context, headers stripped | | `git log` | Hash, author and subject only | | `git add/commit/push` | Confirmation line instead of full progress output | | `cargo test` / `npm test` | Failures only, passing tests collapsed to a count | | `ruff check` | Grouped by rule and file | | `sqlfluff lint` | Grouped by rule and file | | `pytest` | Failures only, traceback trimmed | | `go test` | NDJSON parsed, failures only | | `docker ps` | Essential fields only | ## How Savings Work RTK reduces the **bash output** your agent reads. That is what RTK measures, and it is not the same as cutting your bill by the same amount. Bash output is **one contributor to input tokens**, alongside your prompt, the system prompt and conversation history. Input tokens are in turn **only part of the bill**, which also counts output tokens. The reduction dilutes at every step. The token counts RTK reports are estimated as `bytes / 4` — RTK ships no tokenizer, so the **percentages are reliable but the absolute token numbers are approximate**. > Full explanation: [How RTK Savings Work](docs/guide/resources/savings-explained.md) ## Installation ```bash brew install rtk # macOS / Linux winget install rtk-ai.rtk # Windows curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rtk-ai/rtk/refs/heads/master/install.sh | sh ``` Then check you have the right package — another project named "rtk" exists on crates.io: ```bash rtk --version # any current version rtk gain # must show the savings dashboard, not "command not found" ``` > Cargo, pre-built binaries, native Windows, WSL, and uninstall: **[Installation guide](https://www.rtk-ai.app/guide/getting-started/installation)** ## What You Install RTK ships as three downloads. The two `rtk` editions install a binary with the **same name** — hooks, scripts and agent config work unchanged across both — so they cannot be installed together. Uninstall one before installing the other. ```mermaid flowchart TD agent["Your coding agent"] subgraph editions["Pick one · both install a binary named rtk"] direction LR full["rtk
Apache-2.0 + BUSL-1.1
hooks · filters · engine"] oss["rtk-oss
Apache-2.0 only
hooks · filters"] end proxy["rtk-proxy
BUSL-1.1
compresses API traffic"] agent -->|"command output"| full agent -->|"command output"| oss agent -.->|"API traffic"| proxy classDef apache stroke:#2da44e,stroke-width:2px,fill:none classDef busl stroke:#0969da,stroke-width:2px,fill:none classDef mixed stroke:#8250df,stroke-width:2px,fill:none classDef plain stroke:#8c959f,stroke-width:1px,fill:none class full mixed class oss apache class proxy busl class agent plain style editions fill:none,stroke:#d0d7de,stroke-dasharray:4 4 ``` | Download | Licence | Contains | |---|---|---| | `rtk-` | Apache-2.0 + BUSL-1.1 | Hook core, every command filter, **and** the compression engine | | `rtk-oss-` | Apache-2.0 only | Hook core and every command filter. No engine. | | `rtk-proxy-` | BUSL-1.1 | The RTK Proxy daemon. Never bundled with either `rtk`. | **Production use is free**, engine and daemon included. What the BUSL grant does not cover is offering RTK or a derivative to third parties as a commercial product or service — for that, contact **contact@rtk-ai.app**. ```bash curl -fsSL .../install.sh | RTK_EDITION=oss sh # Apache-2.0 edition brew install rtk-ai/tap/rtk-oss ``` > What the Apache-2.0 edition omits and where the licence boundary falls: **[Editions and Licensing](https://www.rtk-ai.app/guide/resources/editions)** ## Quick Start ```bash # 1. Restart your AI tool, then test git status # Automatically rewritten to rtk git status ``` The agent receives compact output without ever calling `rtk` explicitly. **The hook only fires on Bash tool calls.** Built-in tools like `Read`, `Grep` and `Glob` do not pass through it. Use shell commands (`cat`, `rg`, `find`) or call `rtk read`, `rtk grep`, `rtk find` directly. > Per-agent setup, `--dry-run`, and uninstall: **[Quick Start](https://www.rtk-ai.app/guide/getting-started/quick-start)** · **[Supported Agents](https://www.rtk-ai.app/guide/getting-started/supported-agents)** ## How It Works ``` Without rtk: With rtk: Claude --git status--> shell --> git Claude --git status--> RTK --> git ^ | ^ | | | full raw output | | compact output | filter | +-----------------------------------+ +------- (filtered) ---+----------+ ``` Four strategies applied per command type: 1. **Smart Filtering** - Removes noise (comments, whitespace, boilerplate) 2. **Grouping** - Aggregates similar items (files by directory, errors by type) 3. **Truncation** - Keeps relevant context, cuts redundancy 4. **Deduplication** - Collapses repeated log lines with counts > **Does RTK break Claude's prompt cache?** No. RTK filters output once per command. The result is stored in history and cached normally on subsequent API calls, so the cache keeps working as expected. Smaller outputs also mean cheaper cache writes and reads. readmeHtml:
Agent-agnostic token optimization: compress, route, filter, and more.

One composable pipeline across everything your AI agent reads and sends — built on RTK's battle-tested bash-output compression (up to 90% smaller).

Website • Install • Troubleshooting • Architecture • Discord

English • Francais • 中文 • 日本語 • 한국어 • Espanol • Português

rtk filters and compresses command outputs before they reach your LLM context. Single Rust binary, 100+ supported commands, <10ms overhead.

What RTK Does

RTK intercepts shell commands and compresses their output before your agent reads it.

Operation What RTK does to the output
ls / tree Tree format with file counts instead of one line per entry
cat / read Smart file reading: signatures and structure over full bodies
grep / rg Truncates long lines, groups matches by file
ast-grep Groups structural matches by file, caps overflow
git status Compact stat format, grouped by state
git diff Reduced context, headers stripped
git log Hash, author and subject only
git add/commit/push Confirmation line instead of full progress output
cargo test / npm test Failures only, passing tests collapsed to a count
ruff check Grouped by rule and file
sqlfluff lint Grouped by rule and file
pytest Failures only, traceback trimmed
go test NDJSON parsed, failures only
docker ps Essential fields only

How Savings Work

RTK reduces the bash output your agent reads. That is what RTK measures, and it is not the same as cutting your bill by the same amount.

Bash output is one contributor to input tokens, alongside your prompt, the system prompt and conversation history. Input tokens are in turn only part of the bill, which also counts output tokens. The reduction dilutes at every step.

The token counts RTK reports are estimated as bytes / 4 — RTK ships no tokenizer, so the percentages are reliable but the absolute token numbers are approximate.

Full explanation: How RTK Savings Work

Installation

brew install rtk                                              # macOS / Linux
winget install rtk-ai.rtk                                     # Windows
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rtk-ai/rtk/refs/heads/master/install.sh | sh

Then check you have the right package — another project named "rtk" exists on crates.io:

rtk --version   # any current version
rtk gain        # must show the savings dashboard, not "command not found"

Cargo, pre-built binaries, native Windows, WSL, and uninstall: Installation guide

What You Install

RTK ships as three downloads. The two rtk editions install a binary with the same name — hooks, scripts and agent config work unchanged across both — so they cannot be installed together. Uninstall one before installing the other.

    agent["Your coding agent"]

        direction LR
        full["<b>rtk</b><br/>Apache-2.0 + BUSL-1.1<br/>hooks · filters · engine"]
        oss["<b>rtk-oss</b><br/>Apache-2.0 only<br/>hooks · filters"]
    end

    proxy["<b>rtk-proxy</b><br/>BUSL-1.1<br/>compresses API traffic"]

    agent -->|"command output"| full
    agent -->|"command output"| oss
    agent -.->|"API traffic"| proxy

Loading
Download Licence Contains
rtk-<target> Apache-2.0 + BUSL-1.1 Hook core, every command filter, and the compression engine
rtk-oss-<target> Apache-2.0 only Hook core and every command filter. No engine.
rtk-proxy-<target> BUSL-1.1 The RTK Proxy daemon. Never bundled with either rtk.

Production use is free, engine and daemon included. What the BUSL grant does not cover is offering RTK or a derivative to third parties as a commercial product or service — for that, contact contact@rtk-ai.app.

curl -fsSL .../install.sh | RTK_EDITION=oss sh    # Apache-2.0 edition
brew install rtk-ai/tap/rtk-oss

What the Apache-2.0 edition omits and where the licence boundary falls: Editions and Licensing

Quick Start

# 1. Install for your AI tool
rtk init -g                     # Claude Code / Copilot (default)
rtk init -g --gemini            # Gemini CLI
rtk init -g --codex             # Codex (OpenAI)
rtk init -g --agent cursor      # Cursor
rtk init -g --agent windsurf    # Windsurf
rtk init --agent cline          # Cline / Roo Code
rtk init --agent kilocode       # Kilo Code
rtk init --agent antigravity    # Google Antigravity
rtk init --agent kimi           # Kimi AI
rtk init -g --agent pi          # Pi
rtk init --agent omp            # Oh My Pi (OMP)
rtk init --agent hermes         # Hermes
rtk init -g --agent droid       # Factory Droid
rtk init --agent trae           # Trae (project: .trae/hooks.json)
rtk init -g --agent trae        # Trae global: ~/.trae and existing ~/.trae-cn

# 2. Restart your AI tool, then test
git status  # Automatically rewritten to rtk git status

The agent receives compact output without ever calling rtk explicitly.

The hook only fires on Bash tool calls. Built-in tools like Read, Grep and Glob do not pass through it. Use shell commands (cat, rg, find) or call rtk read, rtk grep, rtk find directly.

Per-agent setup, --dry-run, and uninstall: Quick Start · Supported Agents

How It Works

  Without rtk:                                    With rtk:

  Claude  --git status-->  shell  -->  git         Claude  --git status-->  RTK  -->  git
    ^                                   |            ^                      |          |
    |         full raw output           |            |  compact output      | filter   |
    +-----------------------------------+            +------- (filtered) ---+----------+

Four strategies applied per command type:

  1. Smart Filtering - Removes noise (comments, whitespace, boilerplate)
  2. Grouping - Aggregates similar items (files by directory, errors by type)
  3. Truncation - Keeps relevant context, cuts redundancy
  4. Deduplication - Collapses repeated log lines with counts

Does RTK break Claude's prompt cache? No. RTK filters output once per command. The result is stored in history and cached normally on subsequent API calls, so the cache keeps working as expected. Smaller outputs also mean cheaper cache writes and reads. See Troubleshooting for details.

Supported AI Tools

RTK supports 18 AI coding tools. Each integration rewrites shell commands to rtk equivalents, reducing the bash output the agent reads where the agent supports command interception.

Tool Install Method
Claude Code rtk init -g PreToolUse hook (native binary)
GitHub Copilot (VS Code) rtk init -g --copilot PreToolUse hook — transparent rewrite
GitHub Copilot CLI rtk init -g --copilot PreToolUse deny-with-suggestion (CLI limitation)
Cursor rtk init -g --agent cursor preToolUse hook (hooks.json)
Gemini CLI rtk init -g --gemini BeforeTool hook
Codex rtk init -g --codex PreToolUse hook (updatedInput) + AGENTS.md
Windsurf rtk init -g --agent windsurf .windsurfrules (project-scoped)
Cline / Roo Code rtk init --agent cline .clinerules (project-scoped)
OpenCode rtk init -g --opencode Plugin TS (execute.before / tool.execute.before), needs 1.18.29 or newer
OpenClaw openclaw plugins install ./openclaw Plugin TS (before_tool_call)
Pi rtk init -g --agent pi (global) TypeScript extension (tool_call)
Oh My Pi (OMP) rtk init -g --agent omp (global) / rtk init --agent omp (project) TypeScript extension (tool_call, shared with Pi)
Hermes rtk init --agent hermes Python plugin adapter (terminal command mutation via rtk rewrite)
Mistral Vibe rtk init -g --agent vibe pre_tool hook (hooks.toml)
Kilo Code rtk init --agent kilocode .kilocode/rules/rtk-rules.md (project-scoped)
Google Antigravity rtk init --agent antigravity / rtk init -g --agent antigravity .agents/plugins/rtk/ (project) or ~/.gemini/config/plugins/rtk/ (global): plugin.json, hooks.json, rules/AGENTS.md
Kimi AI rtk init --agent kimi AGENTS.md (project-scoped)
Factory Droid rtk init -g --agent droid (or per-project) PreToolUse hook in ~/.factory/hooks.json (matcher Execute)
Trae rtk init --agent trae Native PreToolUse hook in .trae/hooks.json (RunCommand)
Trae (global) rtk init -g --agent trae ~/.trae/hooks.json, plus ~/.trae-cn/hooks.json when that directory exists

For per-agent setup details, override controls, and graceful degradation, see the Supported Agents guide. The Hermes plugin source and tests live in hooks/hermes/; installed Hermes runtime files still live under ~/.hermes/plugins/rtk-rewrite/.

What RTK Covers

100+ commands across Git, GitHub CLI, Cargo/Rust, JavaScript (npm, pnpm, vitest, jest, tsc, Next.js, Playwright, Prisma), Python (ruff, pytest, mypy, pip), Go (go test, golangci-lint), Ruby, .NET, JVM (Gradle, Maven), PHP, Docker, Kubernetes, AWS, Terraform, and the file/search builtins.

-v, --verbose          # increase verbosity (-v, -vv, -vvv)
rtk bypass <cmd>       # run one command unfiltered, still tracked

Every command and its filter: What RTK Optimizes

Measure It

rtk gain                        # Summary stats
rtk gain --graph                # ASCII graph (last 30 days)
rtk gain --history              # Recent command history
rtk gain --daily                # Day-by-day breakdown
rtk gain --all --format json    # JSON export for dashboards

rtk discover                    # Find missed savings opportunities
rtk discover --all --since 7    # All projects, last 7 days

rtk session                     # Show RTK adoption across recent sessions

Attribution, the live dashboard and export formats: Token Savings Analytics

RTK Proxy (optional)

rtk optimizes command output before your agent reads it. The rtk-proxy daemon extends the same engine to your agent's provider-API traffic — a local background process that sits between your agent and the provider and runs the pipeline on the traffic itself: it compresses payloads, strips bytes no model ever needed before forwarding, and carries the calls your pipeline routes to cheaper models, so they borrow the credential your agent already sends and show up in rtk gain. It can also align prompt-cache breakpoints where the agent leaves them open (opt-in).

rtk claude              # start the daemon if needed, then launch Claude through it
rtk llm-proxy status    # is it up
rtk gain                # savings, command-filtering and proxy side by side

Two independent ways in, because not every harness has a session hook:

What it does
rtk init -g Offers to set it up once: writes the base URL and the rtk:proxy pipeline, then asks how the daemon should come back after a reboot — SessionStart hook, background service, or neither.
rtk <harness> No configuration at all. Starts the daemon, points the harness at it, then execs it. Needs no hook system, which is why it covers harnesses that have none.

rtk <harness> resolving is itself the signal that traffic really goes through the daemon — the subcommand exists only where redirection is verified. Today that is rtk claude. A harness without one is never silently unproxied: it falls through to plain passthrough, and rtk llm-proxy setup lists what can be launched.

It is a separate binary under a separate licence (BUSL-1.1), shipped as its own rtk-proxy-<target> archive — rtk never links it.

Setup and subcommands: RTK Proxy · what it compresses: What the Proxy Compresses · settings and endpoints: Proxy Configuration

The Engine (pipeline.toml)

Everything RTK does — which commands get rewritten, what happens to a tool's output, what the proxy compresses — is expressed in one composable file. The engine (engine/, crate rtk-engine, BUSL-1.1) reads it, so the levers are configurable instead of hard-coded.

Upgrading changes nothing. With no pipeline file you are on rtk:default: the same PreToolUse rewrite, the same awareness file, your filters.toml, your config.toml. Everything beyond that is opt-in, one line at a time:

# ~/.config/rtk/pipeline.toml
[pipeline]
extends = ["rtk:posthook", "rtk:proxy"]

The tour: Pipelines · the reference: Writing a Pipeline, Conditions and Judges, Methods, Tasks and Upstreams · the commands: Pipeline Commands · write your own method: Plugins

Repository references: engine/README.md · proxy/README.md · ARCHITECTURE.md · CONTRIBUTING.md · SECURITY.md

RTK collects no command content and no file contents. Telemetry is anonymous and off by default — it sends nothing until you opt in with explicit consent (GDPR Art. 6 & 7) via rtk telemetry enable, and documented in Telemetry & Privacy.

aiSummary.oneLiner: A high-performance CLI proxy written in Rust that radically compresses shell output to reduce LLM context token usage.
aiSummary.whatItDoes: rtk intercepts standard developer terminal commands and heavily filters their output before it is read by an AI coding agent, significantly reducing token consumption. The tool operates as a remarkably fast, single-binary Rust proxy with virtually zero latency overhead, capable of intelligently summarizing the output of over 100 common development tools. Instead of returning raw, verbose logs from commands like git diff or cargo test, it parses the output and returns highly dense, compacted summaries containing only the essential failure traces or structural metadata. By aggressively truncating redundant text, rtk massively accelerates agent processing times and drastically lowers API billing costs without degrading the agent's contextual awareness.
keyFeatures: Smart output compression: Intercepts verbose terminal commands automatically and rewrites them into highly compact, token-efficient summaries.
Zero dependency Rust binary: Deploys rapidly as a single, incredibly fast Rust executable adding under 10ms of overhead to standard shell commands.
Tool-specific parsing: Contains deep, native understanding for over 100 tools, intelligently extracting only failures from test runners or structural counts from directory listings.
Agent agnostic integration: Operates seamlessly alongside any standard AI coding assistant or CLI by simply acting as a transparent proxy layer.
Massive token reduction: Empirically slashes the raw bash output length ingested by the LLM by up to 90 percent on standard debugging workflows.
